chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Barqi, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, from Fudayl, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who deposited with a man from your mawali (clients/freemen) some wealth of his. The man upon whom the wealth is due is an Arab who is able to withhold it from him, while the depositor is a wicked, outgoing, devilish man. I did not leave out any detail, so he said to me, 'Tell him to return it to him, for he entrusted it to him with the trust of Allah.'

I said, 'And what about a man who bought from a woman from some of the Abbasids some of their plots of land, and he wrote for her a deed, and she has taken the money but has not taken the deed? Should he give her the money or withhold it?' He said, 'He should withhold it from her with the strongest withholding, for she sold what she did not possess.'

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Babawayh (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Our scholars (may Allah have mercy on them) have passed upon that the word of the depositor is accepted, and that he is trustworthy, and there is no oath upon him.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on returning a deposit when the depositee is trustworthy but capable of withholding the wealth?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudence of *wadi'ah* (deposit), emphasizing that the depositee must return the wealth based on the divine nature of the trust (*amanat Allah*), even if the depositor is deemed untrustworthy. It further illustrates the principle of *ghabn* or incomplete possession in sales, where the buyer withholds payment because the seller lacked full ownership at the time of transaction. The concluding note by Ibn Babawayh highlights the Shia scholarly consensus that the depositor’s claim is accepted without an oath, reinforcing the reliability of the entrusted party in such disputes.
